blogs.title: Intrinsic, Not Propensity: The Eighth Circuit’s Expansive View of Prior Gun Possession in United States v. Cutbank
blogs.description: This post would examine the panel’s treatment of testimony that witnesses had seen Cutbank with the same sawed-off rifle before the charged incident. It would analyze the court’s reliance on the ‘intrinsic evidence’ label and on prior-possession doctrine to avoid Rule 404(b), and ask whether the opinion reflects an increasingly broad path for prosecutors to introduce uncharged firearm-related conduct whenever the government can tie it to the same weapon. The piece would also consider what this means for defense efforts to cabin ‘continuous possession’ theories in felon-in-possession cases.

blogs.title: Context, Confrontation, and Harmless Error: Why Cutbank Shows How Hard It Is to Win Evidentiary Appeals
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s handling of the hearsay, limiting-instruction, impeachment, and Rule 403 issues. It would explore the panel’s view that out-of-court statements offered to explain police conduct pose little Sixth Amendment risk once the declarant later testifies, and that trial judges retain wide discretion over timing of limiting instructions and authentication of impeachment material. More broadly, the post would argue that Cutbank is a reminder that evidentiary objections on appeal often collapse into harmless-error review, especially when the government has strong physical and testimonial proof.

blogs.title: When the Firearm Guideline Beats the Armed Career Criminal Guideline: Sentencing Logic in Cutbank
blogs.description: This post would analyze the sentencing portion of the opinion, especially the interaction between ACCA status and the four-level enhancement under USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). The interesting wrinkle is that the non-ACCA firearm guideline calculations, boosted by the ‘in connection with another felony’ enhancement and other adjustments, produced a higher offense level than the Armed Career Criminal Guideline itself. The post would explain why the panel treated Cutbank’s objection as really a substantive-reasonableness argument dressed up as a Guidelines complaint, and what the case says about the limited force of the parsimony principle once the Guidelines range is correctly calculated.

blogs.title: A Quiet Appellate-Practice Lesson in Cutbank: Undeveloped Arguments, Judicial Frustration, and Issue Inflation
blogs.description: This post would take up the opinion’s rhetorical subtext rather than its merits holdings alone. Judge Loken repeatedly notes that Cutbank offered ‘no cases and almost no analysis,’ and pointedly rebukes the government for ‘unnecessarily expand[ing] the issues on appeal.’ The post would explore how federal appellate courts respond when briefing is thin, when objections are only weakly preserved, and when appellees try to litigate issues the appellant barely raised. For practitioners, the case offers a useful study in how briefing quality can shape the depth of appellate review and the court’s willingness to engage doctrinally.
